title: Credit scores
examples: What is the biggest factor when checking my credit score?
How long does it take for a new account to affect my score?
If I pay off a lot of debt, how quickly will my score improve?

explain.say: Today we are learning about what builds a good credit score.

items: New credit accounts can affect it

explain.say: Your payment history shows if you pay bills on time.
The length of your credit history tells lenders how long you manage credit.
How much new credit you use also plays a big role.
In real life, when you get a mortgage, lenders check your score.
A common mistake is ignoring small, recurring utility bills.

faq.q: How quickly does a single late payment hurt my score?
faq.a: A single late payment can cause a noticeable dip in your score. Lenders see it as a sign of immediate risk. You might also ask: How fast is the damage? What is the impact of one missed payment?
asks: Will one late bill ruin my score?
How long does a missed payment affect things?

faq.q: Does only paying off my credit cards help my score?
faq.a: Paying down balances is very helpful because it lowers your credit utilization ratio. This shows you are managing your available credit well. You could also ask: Is paying down debt enough? Will paying balances improve my rating?
asks: Is paying off cards the only way?

faq.q: Do I need a long history to have a good score?
faq.a: While length helps, responsible behavior matters more than just time. A long history of good payments is ideal. You might ask: Does age matter for scores? Can I build a score quickly?
asks: How old should my credit history be?
What is the minimum history length?

faq.q: Are utility bills included in my credit score?
faq.a: Generally, only credit accounts reported to the bureaus affect the score. Utility payments are usually reported separately or not at all. You might ask: Do phone bills count? Do I need a credit card for a good score?

faq.q: If I pay everything on time, can I still lower my score?
faq.a: Yes, opening too many new accounts too quickly can signal risk to lenders. This is called 'credit seeking behavior.' You might ask: What is 'credit seeking'? Can opening accounts lower my score?
asks: What is the danger of many new accounts?

facts: Payment history accounts for a significant portion of your credit score calculation.
Credit utilization, the amount you owe versus your limit, is a key factor.
Establishing a long, positive credit history builds credibility with lenders.
Different lenders use slightly different scoring models.

quiz.say: Which factor has the most immediate impact on a score?
quiz.why: Payment history directly reflects your reliability in paying debts.

wrong.0: Opening new accounts causes a temporary dip due to the inquiry, but payment history is more fundamental.
wrong.1: Credit mix is useful, but timely payments on existing accounts are weighted more heavily.
wrong.3: This factor is important but shows long-term patterns, not immediate reliability.

quiz.say: If you have a high credit limit but use most of it, what happens?

options.show: Your score will stay the same.
options.say: Your score will stay the same.

options.show: Only the credit card company notices.
options.say: Only the credit card company notices.

quiz.why: High utilization signals that you might be over-relying on credit.

wrong.1: Lenders view high usage as a potential financial strain.
wrong.2: This is incorrect; high usage is a warning sign, not a reward.
wrong.3: Credit bureaus and potential lenders track this information.

quiz.say: If a student pays off a large balance right before applying for a loan, what is the best effect?

options.show: It only affects the specific card issuer.
options.say: It only affects the specific card issuer.

options.show: It only helps if the loan is for a car.
options.say: It only helps if the loan is for a car.

options.show: It improves the credit utilization ratio.
options.say: It improves the credit utilization ratio.

quiz.why: Lowering balances relative to your total limit is a positive signal.

wrong.0: The ratio is a key metric lenders analyze closely.
wrong.1: The information is usually reported to the major credit bureaus.
wrong.2: Credit scores are generally used for various types of loans, not just auto.
